Greetings: These two black archived binders contain the wartime letters of Captain Jack Beckerman who was posted to the U.S. Army Forces Far East, or USAFFE in Australia. Between 1941 and 1945, Jack was in the Finance Department, Office of the Fiscal Director. This whole organization was just one of many organizations that comprised the USAFFE under the command of General Douglas MacArthur. Within the two binders are correspondence from Jack to his family including: His younger brother Abe, and younger sister Ruth, as well as letters to his mother and father. If the reader were to take the time and review all of correspondence (and I don't expect that there is enough time in a day to do so), he or she might be transported back in time to 1941 Australia. Jack was very good at describing his surroundings and experiences. Although never in combat, one will get an idea of what Australia was like from 1941-1945. Also, his brother Abe, was drafted in 1943, during boot camp, he wrote some heart felt letters about his feelings for the U.S. Army life and his doubts about being able to kill a man in combat. From Jack and Abe's letters the reader can get an idea of boot camp training and living as both of them went to the same camp, Camp Croft in South Carolina. The reader can also get a feeling for moving about in the military. Jack was able to advance from Private, to Lieutenant, and then Captain. Originally Jack was just another draftee, but because he had a college degree from City College of New York (CUNY) and became an accountant before the war, he was able to transfer those skills to the Finance Dept. in the Far East. However, Abe did not have a degree and lacked any skills the Army could use so he was slated to be an infantryman in a rifle company. In a few of his letters he mentioned to Jack, upon Jack's advice in a previous letter, that he had tried to join the Navy. But at that time, the Navy had all the men it needed and the Army needed infantrymen. So, Abe spent most of active service, also under General MacArthur, but on the Island of Morotai south of the Philippine Islands. In conclusion, I know that there is much correspondence here, I suggest that you skim over everything and maybe along the way you might find something that strikes you eye. Sincerely, James A. Black
